Kennedy starts high school. He is one of the only Catholic students at a predominantly Protestant boarding school in Connecticut.
Kennedy's father becomes U.S. ambassador to the United Kingdom. Kennedy later writes his Harvard senior thesis on the U.K.'s failure to confront the rise of Nazi Germany.
Kennedy volunteers for the U.S. Navy during World War II but is rejected for poor health. Thanks to his father's connections, he is allowed to join the Navy and serves in the South Pacific.

After their boat is damaged, Kennedy leads his men on a 3.5-mile swim to a deserted island where they hide from Japanese patrols. Kennedy receives multiple military awards for his leadership during the ordeal.
At age 29, Kennedy is elected to the U.S. House of Representatives as a Democrat for the 11th District in Boston.
Kennedy is elected to his first term in the U.S. Senate.

contents.text: On September 26, 1960, more than 70 million Americans watched the first-ever televised U.S. presidential debate. Read the passage about the debate between John F. Kennedy and his Republican opponent, Vice President Richard Nixon. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: In preparation for the debate, the Kennedy campaign focused on media strategy as well as debate tactics. Kennedy received advice about his body language and practiced speaking directly into the camera. These efforts paid off: Kennedy came across as confident and capable. In contrast, Nixon, who was recovering from a recent illness and refused to wear any stage makeup, appeared pale, uncomfortable, and untrustworthy.

The difference in the two candidates' appearances left an impression on viewers. Those listening to the debate on the radio felt that while both candidates spoke well on the issues, Nixon won the debate. However, those who watched the debate live on television—including members of Nixon's campaign—felt Kennedy triumphed.

It demonstrated that most voters still preferred to follow politics over the radio, not by television.
It showed that despite new technology, voters did not care about how candidates looked.
It showed that both candidates immediately embraced television as a new way to reach potential voters.

components.text: We observe today not a victory of [political] party, but a celebration of freedom—symbolizing an end as well as a beginning—signifying renewal as well as change.…

We dare not forget today that we are the heirs of [the American] revolution. Let the word go forth from this time and place, to friend and foe alike, that the torch has been passed to a new generation of Americans.…Let every nation know, whether it wishes us well or ill, that we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship, support any friend, oppose any foe to assure the survival and the success of liberty.…

contents.text: The Cuban Missile Crisis came to an end on October 28, 1962, thirteen days after it began. Read the passage about the conclusion of the crisis. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Historians believe the Cuban Missile Crisis is the closest the world has ever come to full-scale nuclear war. Despite repeated threats by both sides that nuclear weapons would be used, the crisis was resolved through diplomatic negotiations. The Soviet Union promised to remove its missiles from Cuba and to allow the United Nations to verify the removal. The United States promised to lift the naval quarantine and never to invade Cuba. This agreement relieved a terrified public and allowed Khrushchev to claim he had successfully protected Cuba from U.S. aggression.

In addition to these public promises, the end of the crisis included a secret pledge by President Kennedy to remove American nuclear missiles from Turkey. Kennedy insisted on keeping this part of the deal a secret because he did not want to look weak to the American public or anger his European allies, who wanted to keep the missiles in Turkey to protect them from the Soviet Union.

textContent.text: Historians believe the Cuban Missile Crisis is the closest the world has ever come to full-scale nuclear war. The Soviet Union promised to remove its missiles from Cuba and to allow the United Nations to verify the removal. The United States promised to lift the naval quarantine and never to invade Cuba. This agreement relieved a terrified public and allowed Khrushchev to claim he had successfully protected Cuba from U.S. aggression.

Kennedy insisted on keeping this part of the deal a secret because he did not want to look weak to the American public or anger his European allies, who wanted to keep the missiles in Turkey to protect them from the Soviet Union.

contents.text: The Cuban Missile Crisis came to an end on October 28, 1962, thirteen days after it began. Read the passage about the conclusion of the crisis. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Historians believe the Cuban Missile Crisis is the closest the world has ever come to full-scale nuclear war. Despite repeated threats by both sides that nuclear weapons would be used, the crisis was resolved through diplomatic negotiations. The Soviet Union promised to remove its missiles from Cuba and to allow the United Nations to verify the removal. The United States promised to lift the naval quarantine and never to invade Cuba. This agreement relieved a terrified public and allowed Khrushchev to claim he had successfully protected Cuba from U.S. aggression.

In addition to these public promises, the end of the crisis included a secret pledge by President Kennedy to remove American nuclear missiles from Turkey. Kennedy insisted on keeping this part of the deal a secret because he did not want to look weak to the American public or anger his European allies, who wanted to keep the missiles in Turkey to protect them from the Soviet Union.

contents.text: After his election in 1960, President John F. Kennedy continued U.S. support for Ngo Dinh Diem's controversial regime in South Vietnam. Diem was a Catholic in a mostly Buddhist nation, and he angered many South Vietnamese people with his anti-Buddhist policies and preferential treatment of Catholic allies. His government used violence against its political opponents, including Buddhist leaders and communist Viet Cong rebels.
The following passage describes increasing tensions between the Kennedy administration and the Diem regime. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: By spring 1963, political tensions within South Vietnam led to a turning point. In May, government forces killed several unarmed civilians at a public celebration of the Buddha's birthday, setting off large protests against the Diem regime. In response, Diem sent soldiers to break up the protests, accusing Buddhist leaders of working with the Viet Cong. In June, a Buddhist monk set himself on fire to protest Diem's violence, gaining international attention.

Increasing international opposition to Diem's violence led President Kennedy to turn against Diem. In September, he approved the South Vietnamese military's plan to overthrow the Diem regime. Two months later, the military staged a coup, assassinating Diem in the process. Kennedy, who had assumed Diem would be exiled, was shocked by his death. Three weeks after Diem's death, Kennedy himself was assassinated. Vice President Lyndon Johnson became president and significantly increased U.S. involvement in Vietnam.

contents.text: After his election in 1960, President John F. Kennedy continued U.S. support for Ngo Dinh Diem's controversial regime in South Vietnam. Diem was a Catholic in a mostly Buddhist nation, and he angered many South Vietnamese people with his anti-Buddhist policies and preferential treatment of Catholic allies. His government used violence against its political opponents, including Buddhist leaders and communist Viet Cong rebels.

textContent.text: By spring 1963, political tensions within South Vietnam led to a turning point. In May, government forces killed several unarmed civilians at a public celebration of the Buddha's birthday, setting off large protests against the Diem regime. In response, Diem sent soldiers to break up the protests, accusing Buddhist leaders of working with the Viet Cong. In June, a Buddhist monk set himself on fire to protest Diem's violence, gaining international attention.

Increasing international opposition to Diem's violence led President Kennedy to turn against Diem. In September, he approved the South Vietnamese military's plan to overthrow the Diem regime. Two months later, the military staged a coup, assassinating Diem in the process. Kennedy, who had assumed Diem would be exiled, was shocked by his death. Three weeks after Diem's death, Kennedy himself was assassinated. Vice President Lyndon Johnson became president and significantly increased U.S. involvement in Vietnam.

contents.text: The Domino Theory describes President Eisenhower's belief that, like a "row of dominoes set up," a country falling to communism will lead its neighboring countries to fall as well. Eisenhower used this theory to explain why the U.S. should try to stop communist expansion in Asia. So, he would likely support these actions:

creating the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization (SEATO) to help eight regional allies defend themselves against communist expansion

contents.text: After his election in 1960, President John F. Kennedy continued U.S. support for Ngo Dinh Diem's controversial regime in South Vietnam. Diem was a Catholic in a mostly Buddhist nation, and he angered many South Vietnamese people with his anti-Buddhist policies and preferential treatment of Catholic allies. His government used violence against its political opponents, including Buddhist leaders and communist Viet Cong rebels.
By May 1963, tensions within South Vietnam reached a turning point. Place the events in order.

innerComponent.text: Diem sends soldiers to break up the protests, accusing Buddhist leaders of working with the Viet Cong. In June, a Buddhist monk sets himself on fire to protest Diem's violence.
In early November, the military stages a coup, assassinating Diem in the process. President Kennedy, who had assumed Diem would only be exiled, is shocked by his death.
In May, government forces kill several unarmed civilians at a public celebration of the Buddha's birthday, setting off large Buddhist protests against the Diem regime.
Three weeks after Diem's death, Kennedy is assassinated. Vice President Lyndon Johnson becomes president and significantly increases U.S. involvement in Vietnam.
The monk's protest gains international attention, and Kennedy eventually turns against Diem. He approves the South Vietnamese military's plan to overthrow the Diem regime.
